chunks: Charge carrier mobility. The question: What is charge mobility?
Mobility tells you how fast a charge carrier moves for a given push from the electric field.
A higher mobility means carriers move faster, so the material conducts better and devices can switch faster.
Carriers keep bumping into vibrating atoms and impurities along the way, and those collisions limit the speed.
Picture walking across a room while pushed by a steady breeze. In an empty room you reach a good steady speed.
In a crowded room you keep bumping into people, and you move more slowly with the same breeze.
The breeze is the electric field, you are the carrier, and the crowd is the vibrating atoms and impurities.
The analogy fails at very high fields, where the speed stops increasing at all.
At low field the lines follow micro E (slope 1 on this log scale). Above a few kV/cm the curves bend over and flatten at v sat , while the dashed line keeps climbing.
Holes are slower at low field but saturate to a similar order of velocity, so the NMOS/PMOS gap closes in short-channel devices.
The hole saturation velocity is somewhat lower than electrons; the exact value depends on the model.
Drift velocity ( v d ): the average speed of carriers along the field. Electric field ( E ): the push on charge, in volts per cm.
Mobility ( micro ): speed per unit field, v d equals micro E , in cm²/V·s. Scattering: a carrier bouncing off a vibrating atom or an impurity.
Doping: adding impurities, which scatter carriers.
In lightly doped silicon, electron mobility is about 1350 cm²/V·s. Apply a field of 100 volts/cm. The drift velocity is 1350 times 100 equals 1. 35 times 10 to the 5 cm/s.
Holes in silicon have a mobility of about 480, so at the same field they drift at 4. 8 times 10 to the 4 cm/s, about three times slower. That is the whole idea.
"Mobility is how quickly carriers drift per unit of electric field: v d equals micro E , in cm²/V·s.
It equals q tau over m^ , so it depends on how long a carrier travels between scattering events and how light it is.
In silicon it's about 1350 for electrons and 480 for holes at room temperature, and it drops with higher temperature from lattice scattering and with higher doping from impurity scattering.
Conductivity is q(n micro n plus p micro p) , and at high field the velocity saturates near 10 to the 7 cm/s."
